title: Beyond the prefix: caches that change the answer
brief: Some caches skip the model altogether. They save the most and carry the most risk: stale answers, near-miss matches and one user's data surfacing for another. How often questions repeat, who shares the cache and how costly a wrong answer is are all open.

blocks.text: Six cache layers, one rule: the key carries the scope

blocks.caption: Only the provider and engine prefix caches leave the answer untouched

What it saves

Yes, and it can be wrong
Tenant or user scope, model id, embedding model id, template, tool configuration and safety-policy versions [[r17]]

Content hash plus embedding model id and version (author inference from the partition rule above)

exact.why: Saves prefill for any repeat, but still calls the model.

para.why: Works for any wording once the prefix is stable.

unique.why: Helps whenever a long stable prefix exists, even if questions are unique.

shared.why: No answer is shared, so no leak path.

multi.why: Per-organization cache. Use per-customer keys for accounting.

low.why: Safe but saves less than a whole-call cache.

high.why: The output is unchanged, so correctness is untouched.

exact.why: Skips the whole call for identical normalized requests.

para.why: A different wording is a different key, so it misses.

shared.why: One key space is fine for public data.

multi.why: The key must carry identity and permission scope or it leaks.

low.why: Stale answers are tolerable until the TTL.

high.why: Stale until TTL unless you invalidate on source change.

exact.why: Hits, but pays the embedding and lookup first.

unique.why: Every miss pays an embedding and a lookup for nothing.

multi.why: One user's answer can surface for another.

high.why: Microsoft warns results can be incorrect, outdated or unsafe.

exact.why: Hits, with the same overhead as any semantic cache.

unique.why: Partitioning also shrinks the pool of possible hits.

shared.why: Partitioning loses hit rate and buys no safety here.

multi.why: Scope, model, template and safety versions keep answers apart.

low.why: Safer than shared at a modest cost in hit rate.

high.why: Still returns a stored answer, so a wrong match remains possible.

exact.why: Skips the embedding call for repeated text.

para.why: Different text is a different key.

unique.why: Little to reuse, little to lose.

multi.why: Vectors hold no permissioned answer, but key on the model version.

low.why: Deterministic, so nothing wrong can be replayed.

high.why: No answer is replayed, so the risk stays low.

blocks.takeaway: The prefix cache is the only layer that never changes the answer. Every layer above it needs a key that carries identity, permissions and versions.

blocks.title: APIM semantic cache with a partition and a rate limit
blocks.code:
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <llm-semantic-cache-lookup
        score-threshold="0.05"
        embeddings-backend-id="llm-backend"
        embeddings-backend-auth="system-assigned"
        ignore-system-messages="true"
        max-message-count="10">
      <vary-by>@(context.Subscription.Id)</vary-by>
    </llm-semantic-cache-lookup>
    <rate-limit calls="20" renewal-period="90" />
  </inbound>
  <outbound>
    <llm-semantic-cache-store duration="60" />
    <base />
  </outbound>
</policies>
blocks.caption: Lookup and store must be paired. A lower `score-threshold` is stricter. Microsoft suggests starting near 0.05 and says values above 0.2 may cause mismatches [[r16]]. The `vary-by` expression partitions by caller subscription. For per-user data, partition by user or tenant. RedisVL uses `distance_threshold` in cosine distance from 0 to 2 (tutorial sample 0.15), a different scale [[r17]].

blocks.title: Cache failure modes and how you would see them

items.symptom: User B receives an answer that names User A's documents
items.cause: The cache key is only the question embedding, with no tenant or user scope
items.fix: Partition by tenant or user, or do not semantic-cache answers built from permissioned data. Re-check access on every hit

items.symptom: Answers cite a policy that was updated last week
items.cause: The TTL is longer than the source changes and entries are not tied to a source version
items.fix: Add the index or source version to the key, keep TTLs short and invalidate on source change

items.symptom: Two questions that differ by one number get the same answer
items.cause: The threshold is too loose, and embeddings treat near-identical questions as the same
items.fix: Tighten the threshold, gate on numbers and entities, and measure the false-hit rate on a labelled pair set

items.symptom: Latency and cost got worse after enabling the cache
items.cause: Hit rate is low, and every miss still pays the embedding, the lookup and the normal call
items.fix: Measure net savings and switch the cache off below break-even

items.symptom: Old answers appear after a model or prompt release
items.cause: Model, template, tool and safety-policy versions are not part of the partition
items.fix: Put every version that shapes the answer into the key

items.symptom: Response timing reveals that another user's prompt was cached
items.cause: Gu et al. detected global cache sharing across users in seven providers, including OpenAI [[r12]]
items.fix: Scope caches per customer. Use per-customer `prompt_cache_key` on GPT-5.6+ and `cache_salt` on self-hosted engines

blocks.text: Not a cache, but cheaper tokens: batch and flex

blocks.caption: Asynchronous and delay-tolerant modes, as of 2026-10-13. Cost and capacity decisions continue in the cost world
head: Mode
Discount
Latency contract
Limits and notes
rows: `.jsonl` file with a unique `custom_id` per request, one model per file, 200 MB upload limit, separate higher limits [[r22]]
Most finish within 1 hour, expire after 24 hours
Up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB. Results kept 29 days [[r30]]

Per-request `service_tier: "flex"`. Capacity is preemptible, so 429 can mean no capacity and 408 means raise the timeout. Unsupported models return 400, a rule Microsoft's priority-processing page dates to 2026-09-25 [[r23]]

quiz.q: In a multi-tenant RAG assistant, User B received an answer that quoted User A's contract. The assistant uses a semantic cache in front of the model. Which cause fits best?
options: The embedding model is too small, so a larger one would separate the two questions clearly
The partition has no tenant or user scope, so an answer from A's documents matched B's question
The score threshold is too loose in general, so only a much stricter value would have prevented it
The provider prefix cache leaked KV tensors between the two organizations that share the endpoint
quiz.explain: A semantic cache returns a stored answer, and without a scope in the key any similar question hits it, whatever data built the answer. A bigger embedding model does not add scope. A stricter threshold reduces matches but does not remove the leak path. Provider prefix caches are per organization and never store answers.

quiz.q: Select everything that belongs in the partition key of a semantic cache for a multi-tenant assistant that uses tools.
quiz.explain: Scope keeps answers apart, the embedding model id keeps vectors comparable, and template and policy versions stop old behavior from being replayed after a release. A trace id is unique per request, so nothing would ever hit. Response length is an output, not an input that defines which answers are interchangeable.

quiz.q: A public product FAQ bot gets many paraphrases of about 200 questions. The content is public and a day-old answer is acceptable. Which choice fits these dials best?
options: Only an exact response cache, because semantic caches are never safe to run for any kind of workload
Only the provider prefix cache, because it never changes the answer and so carries no risk at all
No cache at all, because any staleness is unacceptable for a bot that answers customers
Semantic cache with a strict threshold, short TTL and versioned partitions, plus prefix caching
quiz.explain: Paraphrase-heavy public traffic with a tolerance for staleness is the semantic cache's best case. Keep the threshold strict, partition by versions and keep the TTL short. An exact cache misses paraphrases. The prefix cache alone leaves most of the cost. The stem says staleness is acceptable, so refusing all caching is the wrong trade.

quiz.q: A semantic cache adds an embedding and lookup that cost 3% of one model call, on every request. The hit rate is 20%. A hit costs only that overhead. A miss pays the overhead and the full call. What does an average request cost, as a percentage of a call with no cache?
quiz.explain: Every request pays 0.03. Misses, 80% of requests, also pay 1.0: 0.03 + 0.8 = 0.83, so 83% of baseline, a 17% saving. Break-even is where 0.03 + (1 - h) = 1, so h = 3%. Below that hit rate the cache costs more than it saves, before counting the risk of wrong answers.

takeaways: Only prefix caches leave the answer untouched. Response and semantic caches replace the model's answer
Every answer cache needs a key with scope, model, template, tool and safety versions
Semantic caches pay embedding and lookup on every miss, so compute the break-even hit rate
APIM's `score-threshold` is stricter when lower, and RedisVL uses a different scale
Timing can leak that another user's prompt was cached, so scope caches per customer
